_meta.description: AdaptIQ starter question bank. Each question is a frame: it belongs to a topic, has a difficulty, a stem, 4 options, a 0-based answer_index, an explanation, and an optional 'misconception' id referencing the parent topic's common_misconceptions (the misconception a common wrong answer reveals). The explanation + misconception tags power the reasoning-trace / explainability layer.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of accessing an element at a known index in an array?
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, so the address of index i is computed directly as base + i * element_size. That is constant time.

questions.stem: You insert a new element at the beginning of an array that already holds n elements. What is the time complexity?
questions.explanation: Every existing element must shift one position to the right to make room, which is n shifts — O(n).

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time to search for a given value in an unsorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: With no ordering to exploit, you may have to examine every element, so searching is O(n). This is different from O(1) access by a known index.

questions.stem: Which statement about arrays is TRUE?
options: Accessing by index and searching for a value are both O(1).
Access by index is O(1), but searching for a value in an unsorted array is O(n).
Access by index is O(n) because you traverse from the start.
Inserting in the middle is O(1) because memory is contiguous.
questions.explanation: Indexed access is constant time, but locating a value without knowing its index requires a linear scan of an unsorted array.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity to reach the k-th node in a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Linked lists have no random access; you must follow k pointers from the head, which is O(k).

questions.stem: Given a pointer to the head, what is the time to insert a new node at the front of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: You create the node, point it at the current head, and update the head pointer — a constant number of operations regardless of list length.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine advantage of a linked list over a dynamic array?
options: Insertion or deletion at a known node without shifting other elements.
questions.explanation: Because nodes are linked by pointers, inserting/deleting at a known position only rewires a couple of pointers — no shifting. (Arrays win on random access, cache locality, and per-element overhead.)

questions.stem: Which technique detects a cycle in a singly linked list using only O(1) extra space?
options: Storing every visited node in a hash set.
Floyd's tortoise-and-hare (two pointers at different speeds).
questions.explanation: Floyd's algorithm advances one pointer by 1 and another by 2; if they ever meet, there is a cycle — all in constant extra space. A hash set works but uses O(n) space.

questions.stem: What does every correctly written recursive function need in order to terminate?
questions.explanation: The base case stops the recursion. Without one (or with an unreachable one), the function calls itself forever and overflows the stack.

questions.stem: A recursive function reaches a maximum recursion depth of d. Ignoring other allocations, what is its space complexity?
questions.explanation: Each pending recursive call keeps a stack frame alive, so at depth d there are O(d) frames on the call stack.

questions.stem: What is the minimum number of moves to solve the Tower of Hanoi with n disks?
questions.explanation: The recurrence T(n) = 2*T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1 solves to 2^n - 1 moves.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of the naive recursive Fibonacci (fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)) with no memoization?
questions.explanation: The call tree branches twice at almost every node, giving exponential time (roughly O(1.618^n), bounded by O(2^n)). Memoization collapses it to O(n).

questions.stem: A stack follows which ordering discipline?
questions.explanation: A stack is Last-In-First-Out: the most recently pushed element is the first one popped.

questions.stem: A queue follows which ordering discipline?
questions.explanation: A queue is First-In-First-Out: elements leave in the same order they arrived.

questions.stem: Which task is naturally handled by a stack?
options: Scheduling print jobs in arrival order.
Managing nested function calls (the call stack).
Serving customers in the order they lined up.
questions.explanation: Function calls nest LIFO — the most recent call must return before its caller resumes — which is exactly stack behavior. The other three are FIFO/queue tasks.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of push and pop on a well-implemented stack?
questions.explanation: Both operations act only on the top of the stack, so they are constant time.

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always splits the array in half (log n levels) and does O(n) work merging per level, giving O(n log n) in all cases.

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of quick sort?
questions.explanation: With consistently poor pivots (e.g., already-sorted input with a naive pivot), partitions are maximally unbalanced, degrading to O(n^2). Its average case is O(n log n).

questions.stem: Which of these sorting algorithms is NOT stable in its standard form?
questions.explanation: Standard quick sort can reorder equal keys during partitioning, so it is not stable. Bubble, insertion, and merge sort preserve the relative order of equal elements.

questions.stem: How much auxiliary (extra) space does standard merge sort use on arrays?
questions.explanation: Merging requires a temporary buffer proportional to the number of elements being merged, so standard array merge sort needs O(n) auxiliary space — it is not in-place.

questions.stem: What is the average-case time complexity of insert, lookup, and delete in a hash table?
questions.explanation: With a good hash function and a bounded load factor, these operations are expected constant time.

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of a hash table lookup?
options: It can never be worse than O(1)
questions.explanation: If many keys collide into one bucket (e.g., an adversarial or poor hash), a lookup may scan all of them, degrading to O(n).

questions.stem: Which is a valid strategy for resolving hash collisions?
options: Separate chaining (a linked list per bucket).
questions.explanation: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a per-bucket list; open addressing (probing) is the other main family. Sorting or ignoring keys are not collision-resolution schemes.

questions.stem: Which statement about a standard hash table is TRUE?
options: It keeps keys in sorted order.
It preserves insertion order of keys.
It provides no guarantee about the ordering of keys.
questions.explanation: Hashing scatters keys across buckets by hash value, so a standard hash table gives no ordering guarantees and does not support efficient range queries (a balanced BST would).

questions.stem: In which order does an inorder traversal of a binary tree visit nodes?
questions.explanation: Inorder traversal recurses left, visits the current node, then recurses right (Left, Root, Right).

questions.stem: The height of a node in a tree is best defined as:
options: The distance from the root to that node.
The number of children it has.
The length of the longest path from that node down to a leaf.
The total number of nodes below it.
questions.explanation: Height measures downward to the deepest leaf; depth measures upward to the root. Confusing the two is a common error.

questions.stem: Which data structure is used to implement a level-order (breadth-first) traversal of a tree?
questions.explanation: Level-order traversal processes nodes in FIFO order, enqueuing children as it visits each node — a queue.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about binary trees and binary search trees (BSTs)?
options: Every binary tree is a BST.
Every BST is a binary tree, but not every binary tree is a BST.
A BST cannot have more than two children per node, but a binary tree can.
They are exactly the same thing.
questions.explanation: A BST is a binary tree that additionally satisfies the ordering property (left < node < right). So BST is a special case of binary tree.

questions.stem: An inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits the elements in what order?
questions.explanation: Because every left subtree holds smaller keys and every right subtree holds larger keys, inorder traversal (Left, Root, Right) yields ascending sorted order.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of searching in a balanced binary search tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: In a balanced BST the height is O(log n), and search follows one root-to-leaf path, so it is O(log n).

questions.stem: What is the worst-case search time in a binary search tree that has become completely skewed (like a linked list)?
questions.explanation: A skewed BST has height n-1, so search degrades to O(n). This is why self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) exist.

questions.stem: Where is the smallest key located in a non-empty binary search tree?
questions.explanation: Smaller keys always go left, so following left pointers until you cannot leads to the minimum. (The rightmost node holds the maximum.)

questions.stem: Structurally, a binary heap is which kind of tree?
questions.explanation: A binary heap is a complete binary tree (all levels full except possibly the last, filled left to right), which is why it maps cleanly onto an array.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of extract-min on a binary min-heap of n elements?
questions.explanation: Removing the root and restoring the heap property (sift-down) takes time proportional to the height, O(log n). Only peeking at the min is O(1).

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of peeking at (reading, not removing) the minimum of a min-heap?
questions.explanation: The minimum is always at the root (index 0 in the array), so reading it is constant time.

questions.stem: What is the time complexity of building a heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the standard bottom-up build-heap?
questions.explanation: Although each sift-down is O(log n), a tight analysis over all nodes (most are near the leaves) sums to O(n). Inserting one-by-one instead would be O(n log n).

questions.stem: Which data structure does breadth-first search (BFS) use to manage the frontier?
questions.explanation: BFS explores level by level, so it uses a FIFO queue to visit nearer vertices before farther ones.

questions.stem: Depth-first search (DFS) is naturally implemented using which mechanism?
questions.explanation: DFS dives as deep as possible before backtracking, which matches LIFO behavior — an explicit stack or the recursion call stack.

questions.stem: What is the space complexity of an adjacency-list representation of a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.explanation: You store every vertex plus an entry for every edge, giving O(V + E). An adjacency matrix would instead use O(V^2), wasteful for sparse graphs.

questions.stem: Which algorithm finds the shortest path (fewest edges) between two vertices in an unweighted graph?
questions.explanation: BFS visits vertices in order of increasing distance from the source, so the first time it reaches a vertex is via a shortest (fewest-edge) path.

questions.stem: Which two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to apply?
options: A balanced tree and a hash table.
Constant space and a single loop.
questions.explanation: DP works when an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions of subproblems (optimal substructure) and those subproblems recur (overlapping subproblems), making caching worthwhile.

questions.stem: Memoization, as a dynamic-programming style, is best described as:
options: A bottom-up approach that fills a table iteratively.
A top-down recursive approach that caches subproblem results.
A greedy approach that never revisits a choice.
A way to sort subproblems before solving them.
questions.explanation: Memoization keeps the natural recursion (top-down) but stores each subproblem's answer the first time it is computed. Tabulation is the bottom-up, iterative-table counterpart.

questions.stem: Adding memoization to the naive recursive Fibonacci reduces its time complexity from exponential to:
questions.explanation: Each of the n distinct subproblems fib(0..n) is computed once and reused, so the total work is linear, O(n).

questions.stem: Why might a greedy algorithm fail on a problem that dynamic programming solves correctly (e.g., 0/1 knapsack)?
options: Greedy is always slower than DP.
Locally optimal choices do not always combine into a globally optimal solution.
DP does not require a base case.
questions.explanation: Greedy commits to the best immediate choice; when those choices do not compose into the global optimum (as in 0/1 knapsack), it can be wrong. DP explores the needed combinations of subproblem solutions.
